Newborn Care

Preventing abusive head trauma: safe care when a baby cries

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Violent shaking or an inflicted blow can cause life-threatening injury to a baby. Suspected injury needs immediate medical help. For everyday care, a simple plan for crying, exhaustion and asking for support can help prevent a dangerous moment.

What abusive head trauma means

Abusive head trauma is serious injury to an infant or young child caused by violent shaking, an inflicted blow or a combination of these. “Shaken baby syndrome” is a familiar older term, but it does not describe every way the injury can happen. An impact is not required for violent shaking to be dangerous.

A baby’s head is relatively large and the neck muscles provide limited support. Violent movement can injure the brain and its blood vessels, leading to bleeding, swelling and impaired brain function. The eyes, neck or spine may also be injured, and other injuries such as fractures can coexist.

A brief violent episode can cause severe harm. There is no safe number of shakes or reassuring time threshold. If a baby may have been shaken or struck, seek emergency medical assessment immediately, even when there is no visible bruise or the baby appears to have settled.

Young babies are vulnerable, but normal gentle care is different

Infants, especially those in their first year, are at greatest risk. Abusive head trauma also occurs in older babies and young children. The first months can be particularly difficult for caregivers because crying and sleep disruption can feel relentless, but a crying peak is not an exact timetable for injury risk.

Ordinary gentle rocking, supported cuddling and normal careful handling are different from violent shaking. Support a young baby’s head and neck and keep movements gentle. Do not throw a baby into the air, hit them or deliberately jerk their head to stop crying.

This distinction should reassure someone worried about an ordinary cuddle without excusing forceful handling. If an actual injury, fall or violent movement has occurred, describe what happened honestly to a clinician. An online description cannot determine whether a particular child has been injured.

Symptoms may be obvious or easy to miss

Warning signs can include unusual sleepiness, difficulty waking, poor feeding, repeated vomiting, marked irritability, abnormal movements or seizures. Breathing may become difficult or stop, and the baby may look blue, grey or very pale. Severe injury can cause unresponsiveness or loss of normal movement.

There may be no obvious external injury. Some symptoms resemble illness or feeding problems, which is one reason suspected trauma needs assessment rather than home observation. A baby who becomes quiet after being shaken has not necessarily been soothed; reduced responsiveness may be a sign of brain injury.

Call the local emergency number for a baby who is unresponsive, has a seizure, is difficult to wake, has abnormal breathing or concerning colour change. Tell the dispatcher about any possible shaking or impact. Do not wait for every symptom to appear or try to prove what happened before obtaining help.

Get emergency help and follow current resuscitation guidance

If the baby is unresponsive and not breathing normally, including only gasping, call emergency services on speaker and start CPR with dispatcher guidance. A lay rescuer should not delay to search for a pulse. Put the baby on a firm, flat surface and follow the instructions you receive.

For infant CPR, 2025 AHA/AAP guidance uses the heel of one hand or two thumbs with the hands encircling the chest; the previous two-finger technique was removed. Compress the breastbone at 100–120 times a minute, about one-third of the chest depth, approximately four centimetres, allowing full recoil.

A trained single rescuer uses thirty compressions followed by two breaths, with minimal interruptions. Thirty is a count, not thirty seconds. Breaths are important for infants; if unable to give them, provide compressions rather than doing nothing. Use an AED as soon as available, with paediatric pads or mode if provided, following its prompts. This brief reminder does not replace hands-on training or the dispatcher’s instructions.

While help is coming, protect breathing and give a clear history

Avoid unnecessary movement when head or neck injury is possible, but keeping the airway open takes priority. Tell the dispatcher if the baby vomits, is breathing but unresponsive, or cannot be kept in a position that allows breathing. Follow guidance about positioning and supporting the head and body together.

Do not shake the child to wake them, give food or drink, or put anything in the mouth during a seizure. Keep them away from immediate hazards while waiting for the ambulance. Continue the emergency instructions rather than repeatedly stopping to check whether things have improved.

Tell the clinical team when the baby was last behaving normally, what you saw, any possible shaking, blow or fall and when symptoms started. Share what you know without filling gaps with guesses. Fear or embarrassment should not delay treatment; accurate information helps the team choose urgent investigations and protect the child.

Diagnosis uses the whole clinical picture

Clinicians assess the history, examination and appropriate tests together. They may arrange brain CT or MRI, an eye examination, imaging to look for fractures and blood tests. Different specialists may contribute because brain, eye, bone and other findings require careful interpretation.

Some descriptions refer to a “triad” of brain dysfunction, bleeding around the brain and retinal bleeding. These terms need care: encephalopathy means disturbed brain function, not simply swelling, and subdural bleeding is inside the skull rather than ordinary bruising under the skin. No isolated finding or three-item checklist should be used by a reader to diagnose abuse.

The team considers alternative explanations where appropriate, such as accidental injury, bleeding disorders, birth-related findings or selected metabolic and genetic conditions. A blood test does not rule out every alternative. A thorough assessment takes the pattern, severity, timing and child’s development into account; it is not a judgement to make from one photograph or scan report.

Treatment is tailored to the injuries

Emergency treatment may include support for breathing and circulation, treatment of seizures and close monitoring in intensive care. Some children need surgery to treat bleeding or pressure in the head. Eye injuries and other injuries are assessed and managed by the relevant specialists.

There is no single medicine that instantly reverses traumatic brain damage, but it is incorrect to say that medicines have no role. They can be essential for complications. Likewise, an operation or a drainage device is used when the particular findings justify it, not automatically for every child.

The team should explain the immediate priorities and update the family as information becomes available. At the same time, professionals need to make sure the child will be safe during and after treatment. Medical care and safeguarding assessment can proceed together without waiting for a family to conduct its own investigation.

Recovery may require long-term support

Outcomes vary with the injuries and the child. Some effects are immediately apparent, while difficulties with learning, movement or behaviour may become clearer as development progresses. Possible consequences include seizures, impaired vision or hearing, developmental disability and cerebral palsy; severe injuries can be fatal.

No general article can predict the outcome for an individual child. Ask the treating team what is known now, what remains uncertain and which changes they will monitor. A reassuring early appearance should not be used to cancel recommended follow-up.

Rehabilitation and developmental support may involve physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and feeding specialists, hearing or vision services and educational support. Families also need clear appointments and practical help. Keep a shared record of the care plan so new difficulties can be raised promptly with the appropriate service.

Make a safe plan for moments of frustration

Crying is a normal way for a baby to communicate, and sometimes it continues despite attentive care. Check feeding needs, a wet or dirty nappy, temperature, tiredness and whether the baby seems ill. Gentle holding or soothing may help, but a caregiver cannot always make crying stop immediately.

If frustration is rising, place the baby on their back in a safe cot with a firm, flat mattress and no loose soft items. Step into another room briefly to calm down and check back within five to ten minutes. Remain nearby; do not leave the home or hand the baby to someone who is angry, intoxicated or otherwise unsafe.

Call a trusted adult for relief. If you think you might hurt the child, put them safely down and get urgent help immediately. This is a protective action, not a failure. Persistent or unusual crying, poor feeding or signs of illness still need medical advice rather than being dismissed as a difficult temperament.

Include every caregiver in prevention

Agree in advance that no one will shake, strike or throw the baby, including when they are exhausted or trying to wake them. Explain the safe-break plan to partners, relatives, babysitters and anyone else providing care. Leave practical contact details and make it clear that asking for help is welcome.

Arrange manageable shifts or specific help with meals, older children and rest when possible. Ongoing anxiety, depression, intrusive thoughts, anger or overwhelming exhaustion deserve professional support. A parent does not need to wait until a crisis to tell a maternity, primary-care or mental-health professional that coping is becoming difficult.

If another caregiver’s behaviour makes you fear for a child’s safety, get help from local emergency or child-protection services as appropriate. Do not leave the child in an immediately unsafe situation. Prevention involves dependable support and a clear response to danger, not expecting one person to tolerate unlimited distress alone.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Suspected shaking or inflicted head injury needs urgent assessment even without visible marks.

Diagnosis requires a complete clinical evaluation, not one finding or a simple triad.

Use current local infant CPR training and emergency-dispatch instructions.

How BeMama can help

Before an exhausting evening, choose a safe place to put the baby down, name an adult you can call and agree on how every caregiver can ask for a break.

When to seek help

Call emergency services after suspected violent shaking or a significant inflicted injury, or for unresponsiveness, seizures or abnormal breathing. If you fear you might hurt the baby, put them in a safe cot and get urgent help.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Never shake, strike or throw a baby.
  • A baby becoming quiet after violence may be injured.
  • Give clinicians an honest account and seek help promptly.
  • A short nearby break with the baby safely in their cot is protective.
  • All caregivers need support and a shared safety plan.

Frequently asked questions

Can a brief episode of shaking cause harm?

Yes. There is no safe number of shakes or minimum duration to rely on.

Is normal gentle rocking the same as violent shaking?

No. Gentle supported care is different. Keep movements gentle, support the head and never throw or jerk a baby.

Could a baby be injured without a bruise?

Yes. Serious internal injury may occur without an obvious external mark.

Should I wait because the baby stopped crying?

No. A quiet or less responsive baby after possible shaking may be injured and needs urgent assessment.

Is the old two-finger infant CPR technique still in the 2025 AHA guidance?

No. The guidance uses one hand or two thumbs encircling the chest. Follow current training and emergency-dispatch instructions.

Does a triad of findings automatically diagnose abuse?

No. Specialists assess the entire history, examination, tests and appropriate alternative explanations.

Is there any treatment for the injury?

Yes. Emergency support, medicines for complications, selected surgery and rehabilitation may be needed, although there is no instant reversal of brain injury.

May I put a crying baby down to calm myself?

Yes. Use a safe cot, place the baby on their back, stay nearby and check back within five to ten minutes while arranging support.

What if I am afraid I might hurt the baby?

Put the baby safely down and call for urgent help. Do not remain holding them while you feel unable to keep them safe.

Who should know the safe-break plan?

Every person who cares for the baby, including partners, relatives and babysitters.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
